A few of us are thinking about starting a project in graphical models and causal inference. This is just the first message to get things started.
@Richard Guo @Rajarshi Mukherjee @Rohit Bhattacharya @Zixiao Jolene Wang

This is a bit off-topic, but @Zixiao Jolene Wang can you explain why you used the sepo agent (I think it's this? https://github.com/self-evolving/repo) for the Statlib project? How is it designed, and how is it different from other coding agents (e.g. codex, opencode) and self-improving agent (e.g. hermes)?
There’s already a discussion thread in #general > Discussion: Lean Workspace I think it would be helpful if we move this question there!
I don't have permission to move this out of this channel. Will post a new one there.
Has there been been any developments in the Graphs & Causality project?
@Bo Cowgill the group is working on setting up the architecture for graphs and operations on graphs. We are aiming to upload a first set of codes soon.
Great. Are you pushing to mathlib or statlib?

@Rajarshi Mukherjee — on graph architecture: I have a small standalone Lean 4 development of Pearl's do-calculus that might be relevant input.

Design choices: DAGs carry a rank function with rank_strict_mono : edge u v → rank u < rank v, so acyclicity is structural rather than a separate proof obligation. Undirected walks are an inductive type with fwd/bwd constructors recording edge orientation, and d-separation is decided by a state machine threading the incoming orientation through the walk.

Back-door and front-door adjustment are proven sorry-free for finite discrete models on PMF, with an explicit Bool witness model confirming the front-door statement isn't vacuous. dsep_sound (Verma–Pearl) is still open — I've decomposed it into layers via Lauritzen moralisation rather than direct induction over walks.

Not proposing it as-is; the design choices are mine and may not match what you're building. But if the rank/walk/blocking representation is useful as a reference point: https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa Thanks for the message! I was looking through the DAG definition in your repo https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus/blob/main/PearlDoCalculus/DAG.lean and was wondering about the design choice of requiring [DecidableEq V] specifically. Is there a particular reason you want decidable equality on the vertex type at the level of the DAG structure?

Good catch — you're right that the structure itself doesn't use it. DAG only has edge, decEdge, rank and rank_strict_mono, none of which need decidable equality.

It's there because everything I build on top uses Finset V: parents is Finset.univ.filter (fun u => G.edge u v), and the conditioning sets in d-separation are Finset V too. I put the instance at the structure level so I wouldn't have to thread it through every downstream definition. That was convenience, not a principled choice.

Moving it out to the definitions that actually need it would be cleaner, and would let the graph layer work over vertex types without decidable equality. Is that the direction you're going with the Statlib graph API?

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa Thanks for this. The plan (at least what I had in mind) was to start from more general mixed graphs and not make DAGs central to the development. Happy to hear what what others think about this.

That makes sense — ADMGs are where the completeness results live, and starting from mixed graphs avoids a migration later. I have no stake in DAGs being central; I built that way because it was the smallest thing I could get to work.

On the representation: my Walk type records edge orientation per step (fwd/bwd constructors), and blocking threads that orientation through the walk as a state machine. Adding bidirected edges would mean a third constructor and an extra state — the collider clause is where it changes, since a bidirected edge is always a collider at both endpoints. That part looks mechanical.

What I don't know is whether the moralisation argument survives. Lauritzen's route is stated for DAGs, and I used ancestral closure plus the marriage-edge correspondence to get soundness. Whether that generalises to ADMGs, or whether the general case needs a different proof strategy entirely, is beyond what I've looked at.

If it's of any use: the DAG case is done and sorry-free (#print axioms gives only the standard three), so it could serve as a sanity check for whatever the general development produces — if the general soundness theorem specialises correctly to DAGs, that's some evidence it's stated right.

https://github.com/Johaan70/PearlDoCalculus

@Johan Magnus Aanderaa The moralisation argument extends to ADMGs with a generalization (every collider-connected paths becomes a undirected edge), see https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-9469.00323.
Does you Walk allow duplicated vertices? I'm asking because most standard texts use "paths" (walks without duplicated vertices) to define d-separation, but mathematically it's easier to work with general walks in my opinion.
My plan is to convince people to define walks and d-separation using the matrix algebra introduced here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.15744 (see Section 6.2 for augmentation criterion for m-separation). We still need to have that discussion.

Yes, my Walk is inductive with fwd/bwd constructors and allows repeated vertices. That was deliberate. The moralisation argument I formalised needs it. In Lauritzen's route the collider case produces a marriage edge, and the resulting moral walk can revisit vertices even when the original was a path. I noted it in the file for exactly that reason.
Working with general walks was also easier for the induction, blocking is a state machine threading edge orientation through the walk, and restricting to paths would have meant carrying a no-duplicates invariant through every step.
Thanks for the Richardson reference. I hadn't seen the collider-connected generalisation. If moralisation extends that way, the structure of my soundness proof might survive with the marriage edge construction replaced by the collider-path one.
The matrix algebra approach is new to me and I'll read Section 6.2. One question from the formalisation side. Does the matrix formulation give decidability of separation for free? My current DSeparated quantifies over all walks, which is fine for proofs but not computable. A matrix criterion would presumably fix that.

The matrix formulation allows us to define "types" of walks via polynomials of basic edge matrices (with "addition" being set union and "multiplication" being concatenation). Separability of vertex sets in a graph can then be defined as the corresponding polynomial equating the null set. Is that what you mean by "decidability of separation for free"?
